name: Bartow-Pell Mansion Museum
description: The Bartow-Pell Mansion Museum, the last remaining 19th-century estate in the Bronx’s Pelham Bay Park, is a cultural and educational institution that serves the broader New York City community. The Bartow-Pell Conservancy works to preserve and maintain the historic Greek Revival mansion and carriage house, as well as the museum’s collection, its gardens, and the surrounding landscape, and to interpret the site’s history with innovative and dynamic educational and public programming for students, adults, and families.

name: The Bronx Museum of the Arts
description:
The Bronx Museum of the Arts, or the Bronx Museum, is an art museum with a focus on contemporary and 20th-century American artists. The Bronx Museum has more than 800 paintings, photos, sculptures, and other works of art in its permanent collection. At times, the museum will host special exhibits featuring international artists.

Highlights
Here are some of the "must see" items at Bronx Museum of the Arts.

Henry Chalfant: Art vs. Transit, 1977-1987
The Life and Times of Alvin Baltrop

name: Saint Paul's Church National Historic Site
The Museum of Bronx History (MBH) at the Valentine-Varian House
description: The Valentine-Varian House, which is also the Museum of Bronx History, is a pre-revolutionary era house built in 1758. During the Revolutionary War (1776-1783), the Valentine home was occupied by British, Hessian, and American troops. Except for 11 months between 1775 and 1776, Valentine and his family remained in the house throughout the war. The house, in close proximity to cannons clustered on a nearby hill, miraculously survived several fierce battles. Financial ruin forced Isaac Valentine to sell the home and the 260-acre property to Isaac Varian, a successful butcher and farmer, in 1792. The Varians kept the house for three generations; one of Isaac’s grandsons, also named Isaac, served as New York City’s 63rd mayor, from 1839-1841

name: The Hall of Fame for Great Americans
description:
The Hall of Fame for Great Americans in NYC's Bronx neighborhood is an outdoor sculpture garden on the campus of Bronx Community College. The Hall of Fame is the first of its kind across the entire country. The gallery was designed by well-known architect Stanford White and is a 630-foot open air colonnade with close to 100 busts.

name: City Island Nautical Museum
description:
http://www.cityislandmuseum.org/city-island-walking-tour.html
The City Island Nautical Museum is a weekends-only museum in NYC's Bronx neighborhood that chronicles the history of City Island's boating. At the start of the 1900s, City Island had a worldwide reputation for building the best wooden boats in the world. The museum is dedicated to preserving that history. City Island also had a hand in building military vessels.

Highlights
Here are some of the "must see" items at City Island Nautical Museum.

City Island’s boat-building history exhibit
The massive City Island historical photo exhibit

name: Bertine Block Historic District
description:
Built in the late nineteenth century by Edward Bertine, the
homes are structures featuring nice stonework with orange and tan
brickwork, mostly in the Queen Anne mode. What stands out is
the architectural detail— the gables, arched doorways and windows,
fan lights, ziggurat designs— with each home looking different. They
are exceptional, but visitors must be cautious, for the block also has
a NYCHA- owned and - operated tenement that is an active drug-dealing
scene

name: Bronx Documentary Center
description: The Bronx Documentary Center is a non-profit exhibition space, education center, and community hub in the South Bronx.  four of the BDC's unique spaces will open to the public, including the historic 614 Gallery, the expansive Annex Gallery, the Tim Hetherington Photobook Library—which includes thousands of publications—as well as The Phillip Leonian Darkroom

name: Bronx General Post Office
description:
murals inside; NYC landmark; The Bronx General Post Office at 558 Grand Concourse is a landmark civic building completed in 1937 by architect Thomas Harlan Ellett. Its restrained classical design features monumental arched windows, granite terraces, and symbolic sculptures at the main entrance.

Inside, visitors will see thirteen New Deal–era murals painted in 1939 by Ben Shahn and Bernarda Bryson. These vivid works inspired by Walt Whitman’s poetry, celebrate American workers and remain one of the Bronx’s most important public art collections.

description:
ceiling murals created by immigrant artists; Built in Romanesque style, for a parish founded in 1906, Our Lady of
Mount Carmel Church has breathtaking architecture. The twin-towered
church has a triple portal, a great wheel window, and superb brickwork.
Inside, twelve massive marble columns represent the twelve disciples.
The interior roof shows images of the twelve disciples and many saints.
Numerous beautiful stained-glass windows represent the Joyful mysteries of the Rosary and the flight to Egypt, and some moments of the public life of Jesus and His Resurrection. At the height of its history in the
40's and 50's, more than 40,000 Italians made Our Lady of Mt. Carmel
their parish.

description:
The Maritime Industry Museum at Fort Schuyler is part of the SUNY Maritime College. The museum houses a number of artifacts and exhibits about maritime and sea life in the NYC area dating back hundreds of years. Guests can see intricate ship models, historic artifacts, and a slew of nautical photographs and prints. It is one of the country's biggest maritime collections.

name: Paradise Theater
description: landmarked interior; The 1929 Loew’s Paradise movie palace in the Bronx is reopening in November, reimagined as The Paradise Performing Arts Center. 97 years in the making, The Paradise Performing Arts Center is the second-largest theater in New York State (4,000 seats) after Radio City Music Hall and now has a noble mission: to present a range of artistic voices that mirror the community and expand access to the arts to the widest possible audience.

name: Church of the Mediator
description: Dubbed the “The Little Cathedral of the Bronx,” this Neo-Gothic style church was designed by Henry Vaughan and completed in 1914. It features Tiffany glass windows, a 1927 stained-glass window depicting Jane Addams and Booker T. Washington, a 99-year-old Skinner pipe organ, and terra-cotta altarpieces—the only known work of George Tinworth in the United States.

name: Bronx Music Hall
description: The Women’s Housing and Economic Development Corporation (WHEDco) developed the Bronx Music Hall (BMH) as a performance venue and community cultural center dedicated to honoring, showcasing and cultivating music, dance, theater, and interdisciplinary arts in the Bronx. Designed by WXY, the BMH features a 250-seat flexible performance theater, a Lobby and Exhibit Hall, rehearsal and classroom space, and an outdoor amphitheater and plaza. The BMH is the new permanent home of WHEDco’s Bronx Music Heritage Center (BMHC), founded in 2010 to preserve and promote Bronx music, cultivate Bronx artists, spur neighborhood revival, and provide cultural programs for the community.

name: Bronx River Foodway
description:
one of New York City’s only edible food forests, inside a city-owned park. Located inside Concrete Plant Park in the South Bronx, the Bronx River Foodway is a pilot project of the NYC Department of Parks and Recreation designed to jump-start the imagination, reconnecting communities to use land within the city. The food forest was first established in 2017 and offers access to a variety of edible plants including medicinal plants like echinacea, nut trees like the chestnut, and an assortment of native berries.

From Urban Omnibus: Foraging is not allowed in New York City parks, unless you are plucking sage, squash, or serviceberries at the Bronx River Foodway, a quarter-acre food forest at Concrete Plant Park. Descended from a floating public art project, the Foodway is now offering up its seventh harvest along the Bronx River. In 2023, Sabina Sethi Unni spent a few days sampling the Foodway’s abundant offerings, significant triumphs, and liberatory possibilities where a toxic mix of sewage, trash, urban runoff, and chemical waste once wreaked havoc on local ecologies.

name: Fine Fare Supermarket
description:
Step inside one of the Bronx’s hidden architectural gems: the former Dollar Savings Bank at 2516 Grand Concourse. Completed in 1933 by the noted firm Halsey, McCormack & Helmer, the building reflects the optimism and civic ambition of the Grand Concourse’s Art Deco era. Its monumental limestone façade, geometric ornament, and grand entrance signaled both strength and stability to a community on the rise.

Though today the site operates as a Fine Fare supermarket, many of the landmarked details of the original banking hall remain.

name: Inspiration Point
description: Inspiration Point is a nonprofit cultural arts center in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx. It is part of the Peninsula, a new development on the site of the former Spofford Juvenile Detention Center, and provides space, resources, and opportunities for creative expression across disciplines.

name: La Bodega NY Studio
description: La Bodega Studios is the ultimate destination for unforgettable events and world-class productions. Designed and curated by co-owner Joseph Guerrido, who formed an elite team of top NYC artists to bring his vision to life, this 5,000-sq. ft. soundstage and event venue contains a replica New York City street, with storefronts, stoops, and even a city bus that have provided a unique backdrop for genre-spanning performances and film shoots.

name: BronxArtSpace
description:
Founded and opened to the public in 2010 as a space for art exhibits and performances, BAS is a community-based 501(c)3 non-profit organization committed to supporting local and often under-resourced artists, fostering projects that engage vital social, educational, and political concerns. Through curating group exhibitions, offering a residency program for Bronx artists, and providing meeting space for artist-led workshops and community-based interest groups, BAS combines forces with similar non-profit organizations to enhance the cultural vitality of our immediate and extended Hunts Point neighborhood.

Located in the densest concentration of public housing in the US, BAS creates programs that represent and inspire its community. BAS works to ensure that Bronx-based artists comprise at least 45% percent of exhibiting artists, and that both women and artists of color are the majority of those presented through our programming.

name: High Pumping Station
description: AI: Tied to the Croton water system and adjacent to High Bridge. Romanesque revival architecture that looks almost medieval. A hidden architectural gem.

name: Fonthill Castle
description: AI: A literal castle overlooking the Hudson at the College of Mount St. Vincent. It feels improbably European in Riverdale. Pair with nearby waterfront walks.

name: Van Cortlandt Park - 242 St
description:
AI: The northern terminal of the 1 train and one of the most atmospheric elevated stations in NYC. The steelwork, the wooden platforms, the open sky above Van Cortlandt Park — it feels old New York in the best way. Pair it with a walk into the park or toward Woodlawn Cemetery for a perfect Bronx afternoon.

Most evocative station on this list.

name: Saint Peter's Episcopal Church and Cemetery
description: AI: Dating back to colonial-era parish roots, this Westchester Square complex blends church, chapel, and cemetery into one deeply layered historic site. The stone buildings and sloping graveyard create a strong sense of continuity.

name: Grand Concourse Historic District
description: AI: The Bronx’s Art Deco spine. Streamlined Moderne apartment houses, geometric detailing, real 1930s glamour. Walk between 161st and 167th for the strongest concentration.

name: Pelham Bay Park
description:
AI: NYC’s largest park — three times the size of Central Park. Forest trails, rocky shoreline, salt marsh, historic estates (Bartow–Pell), and sweeping views toward Long Island Sound. It feels genuinely expansive and sometimes almost rural.

Most landscape-diverse and essential on this list.

name: Ferry Point Park
description: AI: Massive open waterfront space with dramatic Whitestone Bridge views. Windy, open, and surprisingly calming. Less wooded than Pelham Bay, but the skyline and bridge backdrop give it visual punch.

name: Givans Creek Woods
description: AI: A quiet marsh and woodland preserve along a tidal creek. More ecological than dramatic, but rewarding if you like birding and peaceful shoreline paths.

name: Spuyten Duyvil Shorefront Park
description: AI: A long, breezy waterfront path hugging the Hudson. Bridge views, river traffic, open sky. It’s one of the Bronx’s most cinematic linear walks — especially near sunset.

name: Henry Hudson Park
description: AI: Small but dramatic — perched above the river with Henry Hudson Bridge views. Compact, but the setting does the heavy lifting.

name: Aqueduct Walk
description: AI: A quiet green corridor following the Old Croton Aqueduct route. Not dramatic, but historically layered and peaceful.

name: Barretto Point Park
description: AI: Unexpected East River waterfront views toward Queens and Rikers Island. Open sky, salt air, and dramatic bridge backdrops. It feels far removed from Manhattan’s manicured riverfronts — raw and wide open.

name: Crotona Park
description: AI: The South Bronx’s grand old park. Rolling hills, a lake, mature trees, and real scale. It’s one of the borough’s most satisfying inland green spaces — especially beautiful in autumn

name: Van Cortlandt Park
description:
AI: The heavyweight here. One of NYC’s largest parks, and it feels it—real forest, broad meadows, a historic house, and long, uninterrupted trails. Parts of it genuinely feel outside the city. It’s not manicured or showy; it’s about space and variety.
Best for: a proper walk or half-day escape.
Pairs well with: nearby Riverdale views or the Hudson.

name: Bronxlandia
description:
A historic rail station is making new history for the South Bronx.

Although the years have not been kind to this 100+ year-old Cass Gilbert-designed structure, it endures in ruinous grace. It's an early American example of steel-reinforced concrete construction that served as a rail station for its first 27 years and then was subdivided into retail storefronts when rail service was shut down.

Most recently, local resident, MacArthur Fellow, Peabody Award winner, author and Princeton University professor Majora Carter acquired the building from Amtrak and has set about working on its revitalization, now operating it as Bronxlandia, an exciting event venue.
